lesson.title: What a tax takes

steps.headline: A tax drives a wedge between what buyers pay and what sellers keep.

lead.text: Sellers hand the tax to the government on every unit, so what they keep is the buyers' price minus the tax. They decide how much to supply from what they keep. To find the new equilibrium, put P − tax in place of P in the supply equation.

reveal.text: You found that buyers pay £24 and sellers keep £18. The £6 tax is shared: £4 to buyers and £2 to sellers.

lead.text: Coffee sellers must hand over £6 on every cup. Their supply now depends on the price they keep, which is the buyers' price minus 6.

steps.headline: Demand is Qd = 60 − 2P and supply is Qs = 2P − 20. A £4 tax is collected from sellers. Find the buyers' price, the quantity and the revenue.

workedSteps.text: Sellers keep P − 4, so supply in terms of the buyers' price changes.
Find the quantity, then the revenue.

steps.headline: A tax raises revenue on the units still sold and destroys surplus on the rest.

lead.text: Tax revenue is the tax per unit times the units still sold. The trades the tax stops were each worth more to buyers than they cost sellers. That lost surplus is a triangle called deadweight loss: half of the tax times the fall in quantity.

steps.headline: With the £6 tax, coffee sales fall from 60 to 52 cups a day. Find the revenue and the lost surplus.

workedSteps.text: Tax per cup times the cups still sold gives the revenue.
Half of the tax times that fall gives the deadweight loss.

reveal.text: Trade fell below its old level, as it does with any per-unit tax. The units that vanished are where the deadweight loss sits.

lead.text: A new market, the same moves: find the buyers' price with the tax, then the quantity.

reveal.text: Buyers' price rises from £25 to £27: they bear £2 of the £6, against £4 in the coffee market. The side that can more easily walk away bears less.

lead.text: Now gym passes, where buyers are more price-sensitive than sellers. The same £6 tax is collected from sellers. Compare what happens to the price buyers pay.

lesson.orientation: Work out what a per-unit tax does to prices and revenue. Then measure the surplus it destroys and find who bears it.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: A £6 tax on every cup of coffee is collected from the sellers.

intro.promise: By the end you'll find the price and quantity after a per-unit tax, and say who bears it and what it destroys.

recap.keyIdea: A per-unit tax splits the price into what buyers pay and what sellers keep. It raises revenue on units still sold, destroys surplus on units that stop trading, and falls more on the side that finds it harder to walk away.

blocks.text: You found buyers paying £24 and sellers keeping £18, £312 of revenue and £24 of lost surplus. In the gym market buyers carried only £2 of the £6.

recap.nextHook: Taxes are one way to change a market. Next: price controls, and costs that fall on people outside the trade.

questions.prompt: A £6 tax per cup is collected from coffee sellers. Demand is Qd = 100 − 2P, and supply in terms of the price sellers keep is Qs = 4P − 20. What price do buyers now pay, in pounds?
hints: Sellers keep the buyers' price minus the tax.
Replace P in the supply equation by (P − 6) and set it equal to demand.
Solve for the buyers' price.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Sellers keep P − 6, so 100 − 2P = 4(P − 6) − 20 gives 144 = 6P and P = £24.

questions.onCorrect: £24. Replace P with P − 6 in supply, set it equal to demand and solve for the buyers' price.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the price sellers keep. The question asks what buyers pay.
That is the price before the tax. The tax pushes the buyers' price up.

questions.prompt: Tax revenue per day, in pounds
hints: Revenue is the tax per unit times the units taxed.
Use the quantity after the tax, not before.
Multiply the two.
questions.onCorrect: £312. Tax per cup times the cups still sold.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the tax per cup. Multiply by the cups taxed.
That uses the quantity before the tax. Taxed cups are the ones still sold.

questions.prompt: Deadweight loss, in pounds per day
hints: The loss is a triangle between the curves over the units no longer sold.
Its height is the tax wedge and its base is the fall in quantity.
Take one half × base × height.
questions.onCorrect: £24. Half of the tax times the fall in quantity.

misconceptions.feedback: That forgets the half. A triangle's area is half of base times height.
That is the base only. Find the area.

questions.prompt: Demand is Qd = 120 − 4P and supply is Qs = 2P − 30. A £6 tax is collected from sellers. By how many pounds does the price buyers pay rise?
hints: Find the equilibrium price without the tax.
Find the buyers' price with the tax by replacing P with (P − 6) in supply.
Subtract the first price from the second.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Without the tax 150 = 6P gives £25. With it, 120 − 4P = 2(P − 6) − 30 gives 162 = 6P, so £27: a rise of £2.

questions.onCorrect: £2. Buyers who can easily walk away bear less of the tax.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the price before the tax. Find how much it rises.
That is the price after the tax. The question asks for the rise.
That is the whole tax. Buyers' price rises by less than that.

questions.prompt: Demand is Qd = 90 − 3P and supply is Qs = 3P − 30. A £4 tax is collected from sellers. How many units are traded after the tax?
hints: Replace P in the supply equation by the price sellers keep.
Solve for the buyers' price.
Substitute that price into demand.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 90 − 3P = 3(P − 4) − 30 gives 132 = 6P, so buyers pay £22 and Q = 90 − 66 = 24.

questions.onCorrect: 24 units. Find the buyers' price with the tax, then put it into demand.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the buyers' price. Substitute it into demand to find the quantity.
That is the quantity before the tax. The tax reduces trade.

questions.prompt: Without a tax 30 units are traded; a £4 per-unit tax cuts trade to 24 units. Both curves are straight lines. What is the deadweight loss, in pounds?
hints: Identify the units that are no longer traded.
The triangle's height is the tax per unit.
Take one half × base × height.
questions.onCorrect: £12. Half of the tax per unit times the units no longer traded.

misconceptions.feedback: That forgets the half. A triangle's area is half of base times height.
That is the fall in quantity only. Find the area of the triangle.

questions.prompt: Coffee sells for £10 a cup. The government collects a £6 tax per cup from sellers, and the price buyers pay rises to £14. How many pounds per cup do sellers lose compared with before?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Sellers keep 14 − 6 = £8, down from £10: a loss of £2.

hints: How much of the price buyers pay goes to the government?
Take the tax off the new price to find what sellers keep.
Compare that with the old price.
questions.onCorrect: £2. Sellers keep the buyers' price minus the tax. The tax is shared, not passed wholly to buyers.

misconceptions.feedback: That is how much more buyers pay. Compare what sellers keep with the old price.
That is the whole tax. Sellers keep the price buyers pay minus the tax.
That is what sellers keep. The question asks how much less that is than before.

questions.prompt: A £6 tax per cup is collected from sellers. Buyers pay £20 a cup. What do sellers keep per cup?

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Sellers keep the buyers' price minus the tax: 20 − 6 = £14.

hints: The tax comes out of what sellers receive.
questions.onCorrect: £14. The tax drives a wedge: sellers keep the buyers' price minus the tax.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the tax. The tax is taken out of what sellers receive.
That is the tax itself, not what remains after paying it.

questions.prompt: Why change P only in the supply equation?

choices.label: Supply depends on what sellers keep; demand depends on what buyers pay.
Demand is never affected by anything.
Taxes only change the intercept of demand.

acceptedIdeas: Supply depends on what sellers keep; demand depends on what buyers pay.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Buyers react to the price they pay, which is P. Sellers react to the price they keep, which is P minus the tax.

hints: Who reacts to which price?
questions.onCorrect: Buyers react to what they pay, sellers to what they keep. Only supply needs P − tax.

misconceptions.feedback: Demand moves with other causes. Here the point is that buyers react to the price they pay.
The tax is collected from sellers, so it enters through the price they keep.

questions.prompt: Which cups make up the deadweight loss of a tax?

choices.label: The cups no longer traded because of the tax.
The cups still traded after the tax.
The cups the government collects tax on.

acceptedIdeas: The cups no longer traded because of the tax.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The lost trades were worth more to buyers than they cost sellers, and the tax stopped them.

hints: Which trades does the tax prevent?
questions.onCorrect: The trades the tax stopped. Each was worth more to a buyer than it cost a seller.

misconceptions.feedback: Those cups still bring surplus, though less of it. The loss is on the trades that vanished.
Those are the cups that still sell. The lost surplus lies on the ones that do not.

questions.prompt: Demand is Qd = 100 − 4P and supply is Qs = 4P − 20. A £4 tax is collected from sellers. How much tax revenue is raised, in pounds?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: 100 − 4P = 4(P − 4) − 20 gives 136 = 8P, so buyers pay £17 and Q = 100 − 68 = 32. Revenue is 4 × 32 = £128.

hints: Replace P in supply by the price sellers keep and solve for the buyers' price.
Put that price into demand to find the quantity.
Multiply the tax per unit by the quantity.
questions.onCorrect: £128. Solve for the buyers' price, find the quantity, then multiply by the tax.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the quantity traded, not the revenue.
That is the buyers' price. Revenue is the tax times the quantity.
That uses the quantity before the tax. Taxed units are the ones still sold.

questions.prompt: Demand is Qd = 70 − 2P and supply is Qs = 3P − 30. A £5 tax is collected from sellers. By how many pounds does the price buyers pay rise?

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Without the tax 100 = 5P gives £20. With it 70 − 2P = 3(P − 5) − 30 gives 115 = 5P, so £23: a rise of £3.

hints: Find the equilibrium price without the tax.
Find the buyers' price with the tax by replacing P with the price sellers keep.
Subtract the first price from the second.
questions.onCorrect: £3. Buyers carry most of the tax here, because supply is the more responsive side.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the price after the tax. The question asks for the rise.
That is the price before the tax. Find how much it rises.
That is the whole tax. Buyers do not bear all of it.
